The manipulation of time in this excerpt—which serves as the opening to Theodor Fontane's novella *Unterm Birnbaum*—is masterfully balanced to set the scene, establish character, and build subtle suspense. 

The narrative primarily uses the **stretching of time** to transform a very brief, mundane action—Abel Hradscheck walking from the street, through his hallway, and into his garden—into a detailed exploration of the setting and his psyche. As he walks through the hallway, real-time action pauses (stretches) to describe the layout of the house, the barrels, the trapdoor to the cellar, and the **compressed** backstory of how his pretentious wife demanded a separate entrance for the shop. This stretching is entirely appropriate because the physical layout of the house and garden (such as the cellar trapdoor and the pear tree) will be crucial to the plot later on. 

Furthermore, as Hradscheck walks through the garden, the slow, stretched pacing mirrors the sleepy autumn atmosphere and allows the reader to slip into his anxious internal monologue ("And all this was his! But for how much longer?"). When the ripe pear suddenly falls with a heavy thud, it snaps both Hradscheck and the reader back into real-time, seamlessly transitioning into the natural, real-time pacing of his dialogue with his neighbor, Widow Jeschke.
